Sigmund Haas

From the deserts of North Africa to the cockpit of a Mosquito: the wartime story of Zygmunt “Sigmund” Haas, Polish pilot in RAF service.

Part I · Before the Mosquito

A young man from a borderland at war

Zygmunt Haas was born on 25 March 1921 in Czerniowice - then in Romania, today Chernivtsi in Ukraine. His surviving Polish Air Force personnel entry identifies him by RAF service number 704205, records him as a pilot, and gives his final RAF rank as Warrant Officer.1

His U.S. obituary names his parents as Adolf Haas and Franciszka Czownicka Haas. The surviving military record places Haas in the Polish armed forces in exile and later in the Polish Air Force under RAF operational command.

North Africa before the RAF

Before entering RAF operational service, Haas served with the Polish Carpathian formation in North Africa. Historical records place him among the Carpathians during the Tobruk period. He later entered the Polish Air Force training pipeline and flew Mosquito fighter-bomber operations with No. 305 Squadron in northwest Europe.

The Carpathians and Tobruk

A Polish Air Force historical source commemorating the relief of Tobruk lists Zygmunt Haas (later 305 Squadron) among the men who were then in the ranks of the Polish “Karpatczycy” - the Independent Carpathian Rifle Brigade. The same paragraph explicitly notes that another future airman on the list, Jerzy Główczewski, did not fight at Tobruk; it gives no such qualification for Haas.2

The available evidence places Haas with the Carpathian formation during the Tobruk period. His individual army service sheet has not yet been located, so his company, duties, and exact actions in the Tobruk perimeter remain unconfirmed.

His wartime path ran from the Polish Carpathians in the desert to a two-seat Mosquito fighter-bomber over northwest Europe.

From soldier to airman

At some point after the North African phase, Haas entered the Polish Air Force training pipeline in Britain. By August 1944, the history of No. 305 Polish Bomber Squadron records six crews arriving from No. 18 Operational Training Unit. Among them were Sgt Pilot Zygmunt Haas and navigator Tomasz Wilczewski.3

That pairing matters. A Mosquito fighter-bomber carried only two men: the pilot and navigator. There was no large bomber crew around them. On low-level and night intruder work, the two men depended intensely on one another for navigation, target finding, timing, threat awareness and the long route home. Surviving 305 Squadron gallery captions repeatedly associate Haas and Wilczewski as a crew.7

Part II · No. 305 Squadron

The Mosquito war

By the time Haas joined 305 Squadron, the unit had become a fast tactical striking force of the RAF's Second Tactical Air Force. Its de Havilland Mosquito FB.VI aircraft were used for night harassment, armed reconnaissance, bombing and strafing against German transportation and battlefield infrastructure.

No. 305 Squadron. Squadron group photograph supplied for this biography. This is Haas's squadron in France.
Mosquitos at Épinoy, France. No. 305 Squadron aircraft at Épinoy, Haas's base during the documented November 1944 and February 1945 operations.
2 menPilot + navigator in an FB.VI crew
4 × 20 mmForward-firing Hispano cannon
4 × .303Forward-firing machine guns

The Mosquito was fast, light and largely wooden. In 305 Squadron service it could carry 500-pound bombs while retaining formidable forward-firing armament. This made it well suited to the squadron's late-war work: finding railways, trains, road traffic, bridges and other targets, striking quickly, and escaping before German defenses could concentrate.

In September 1944, soon after Haas arrived, the squadron flew nine night operations involving 119 aircraft. The unit's mission remained the destruction of enemy communications and reserves and the disruption of German crossings during the fighting for access to Antwerp. These figures describe the squadron as a whole, not Haas's personal tally.3

Part III · Documented combat episodes

Two times the Mosquito came home badly hurt - or not at all

Night of 25/26 November 1944

HP913 / SM-W - flak, darkness and a parachute escape

The 305 Squadron history places Haas and Wilczewski on a patrol in the Enschede area, where they encountered very strong and accurate anti-aircraft fire. Their aircraft was damaged and the crew abandoned it by parachute. Both men reported back to the squadron the following day.3

Independent Mosquito airframe records identify the aircraft as de Havilland Mosquito FB.VI HP913, squadron code SM-W. They record it as damaged by flak on a night intruder operation over Germany and abandoned near Reims, with both Haas and Wilczewski safe.4

A later specialist account adds the dramatic detail that HP913 suffered an electrical failure after being hit over the Ruhr. Without cockpit lighting, the crew could not properly read their map. According to that reconstruction, they headed south, kept the aircraft airborne until the fuel was exhausted, and then bailed out over Champagne.12 Because that detail comes from a later secondary account, it should be treated as a strong lead rather than the equivalent of an original operations report.

Documented: Haas + WilczewskiDocumented: HP913 / SM-WSecondary detail: electrical failure
22 February 1945

Operation Clarion - home on one engine

Operation Clarion was a massive Allied daylight assault on Germany's transportation network. No. 305 Squadron sent 19 Mosquitos. The unit history lists Haas and Wilczewski as crew number six.3

The squadron was assigned a sector near the Danish-German frontier and instructed to attack targets of military value - roads, railway lines, barges and ships, bridges, junctions, stations, communications installations, gas and water facilities, military quarters, factories and vehicles. Across the 305 Squadron force, crews dropped 33 × 500-lb bombs and fired 7,230 cannon rounds and 5,400 machine-gun rounds.3

A later Polish historical account gives the most vivid description of Haas and Wilczewski's individual attack. They found a long German freight train standing at Warstade railway station. Haas dropped two bombs on the train, then came back around and strafed the railway cars with the Mosquito's forward-firing guns. Explosions and fires followed. He turned back several times for additional strafing passes even as German anti-aircraft fire intensified. During the attack, flak knocked out one of the Mosquito's engines.14

With one engine stopped, Haas flew NT234 / SM-E back across the front and landed at Epinoy. The 305 Squadron history independently confirms his one-engine return and then records the decoration earned for the operation: Sgt Pilot Zygmunt Haas was awarded the Silver Cross of the Order of War Virtuti Militari.35 His service number 704205 also appears on the Polish Air Force list of Silver Cross recipients.6

Documented: Operation ClarionDocumented: returned on one engineDocumented: Virtuti Militari

The winter tempo

Haas's named incidents sit inside a much larger operational campaign. In December 1944 the squadron flew 168 aircraft sorties on 11 operations. Christmas Eve and Christmas Day were spent attacking German reserves and rail traffic; seven crews flew twice within eight hours. In January the squadron put up 147 aircraft over 11 operations. In February it committed 190 aircraft, including 18 on daylight operations. The history notes that crews sometimes flew two sorties in a day.3

By March, 305 Squadron was using Mobile Radar Control Post bombing, allowing Mosquitos to be guided toward targets at night or in poor weather. The unit flew 212 sorties in 19 night operations that month. April was even more intense: 263 aircraft in 23 operations, with patrols reaching the Bremen and Magdeburg areas and even Berlin. Those figures are unit activity; without the original Form 541 crew sheets, they cannot be turned into a personal Haas mission count.

Part IV · The last weeks

Still flying as Germany collapsed

On the night of 25/26 April 1945, 305 Squadron sent twelve aircraft on harassment operations in the Westerland-Flensburg region. The unit history calls it the squadron's final operational night of the war. Five of the twelve crews were Polish.

One entry gives the pilot as “Zbigniew Haas” with navigator T. Wilczewski.3 No separate 305 Squadron pilot named Zbigniew Haas has surfaced in this research, while Tomasz Wilczewski was Zygmunt Haas's established navigator. It is therefore highly plausible that this is a first-name error for Zygmunt - which would place Sigmund on the squadron's very last combat operation - but it should remain labeled probable until the original Operations Record Book entry is inspected.

Combat record

By the end of the war, Haas had survived the loss of one Mosquito after flak damage, returned from Operation Clarion in another damaged Mosquito on one engine, received the Silver Cross of the Virtuti Militari, and remained associated with operational flying into the final weeks of the European war.

Operational sortie total

The surviving secondary sources do not provide a verified personal sortie total for Haas. They do show that he remained operational for months with No. 305 Squadron and that his combat service included repeated night and daylight intruder operations.3

A definitive count requires a crew-by-crew tally of the original No. 305 Squadron Form 541 “Detail of Work Carried Out” records, The National Archives reference AIR 27/1672.8

Part V · Decorations and aircraft

A small personnel entry with a remarkable set of abbreviations

Krzystek's List records Haas's decorations as “VM V kl., KW, 2xML”: Virtuti Militari Class V, the Cross of Valour, and two Air Medals.1

Virtuti Militari - Class V / Silver Cross

Poland's premier military decoration for valor. The 305 Squadron history explicitly records Haas receiving the Silver Cross for the 22 February 1945 Clarion operation.

Krzyż Walecznych - Cross of Valour

Recorded on his Polish Air Force personnel entry. The specific award citation has not yet been located.

2 × Medal Lotniczy - Air Medal

Two awards are recorded. The underlying award paperwork remains a useful target for future archival research.

Final RAF rank: Warrant Officer

During the named 1944-45 operations he appears at lower NCO flying ranks; his personnel entry records W/O as his RAF rank.

Aircraft tied to the Haas-Wilczewski crew

HP913 / SM-W - lost after flak damage on 25/26 November 1944; Haas and Wilczewski bailed out safely. NT234 / SM-E - hit by flak during Operation Clarion on 22 February 1945 and brought home on one engine. An archived 305 Squadron photo caption also identifies HR346 / SM-K as an aircraft flown by the Wilczewski-Haas crew.7

RAF crews did not necessarily “own” one airplane, so these should be read as aircraft associated with particular sorties or photographs, not as Sigmund's permanent personal Mosquito.

Archival photographs

The biography now includes the user-supplied No. 305 Squadron group photograph and the Mosquitos at Épinoy image, along with additional contextual archival photographs. Captions identify whether each photograph is directly connected to Haas or is included as period context.

In addition to the photographs reproduced here, an archived 305 Squadron gallery preserves captions for a Haas-Wilczewski crew photograph and an in-flight SM-K image from Tomasz Wilczewski's archive. Those specific image files currently return 404 errors, but the captions remain useful evidence and are noted in the source list.
